legacy_conversion_note: The original docx (source/Y2/Session 5/Foreign Travel/Case Study_ Foreign Travel.docx) is a real, non-fictional Acton Academy case: two named sisters (Natalie and Katie Majors) planning a real nine-day European itinerary (London -> Dover -> Paris -> Amsterdam -> Groningen -> Brussels -> Canterbury -> Gatwick), dated March 27-April 4, 2026, choosing between renting a car or traveling by rail. Unlike most legacy cases in this corpus, the original docx contained NO embedded numeric data at all -- its four appendices were purely external reference LINKS (a Priceline car-rental search URL, the Eurostar/National Rail websites, tfl.gov.uk, ratp.fr, three general travel-advice articles) with no price tables, fare tables, or schedules reproduced in-document. The accompanying 'Car Rental compressed.pdf' is a screenshot capture of a Priceline search results page from an unknown historical date; its extracted text is font-garbled/unusable (confirmed via python pypdf extraction -- garbled Unicode substitution cipher-like output) and, even if legible, would show rental prices as they stood on whatever day that screenshot was taken, not current data -- it was reviewed and NOT used as a source for this conversion. This conversion therefore did not have any legacy numbers to verify or refresh -- every price, fare, distance, exchange rate, and date fact in case.md was independently researched fresh via WebSearch (all 30 entries in sources[] below) as of August 2026, and the trip dates were shifted forward one calendar year (to the equivalent Friday-to-Saturday window in 2027, see Appendix E's Modeling Assumption E1) purely so the story's own 'in a few weeks' framing (a February conversation about a late-March trip) remains a near-future scenario relative to a student reading this case after August 2026, not a trip that already happened. The day-of-week pattern, the full 9-day city sequence, both named options (rent a car vs. travel by rail), the shared-cost/no-switching-partway constraint, and the general shape of Challenge 3's deliverables (a total transportation cost, a complete timed itinerary, a Channel-crossing decision for the car option, at least one original visual display) are all preserved from the original docx. Two structural facts this case adds beyond the legacy source, both real and independently verified: (1) the UK's British Summer Time and the EU's daylight-saving-time both begin on the exact same date every year (the last Sunday in March) -- meaning the London-to-mainland-Europe one-hour time offset used throughout this case's Appendix B never actually changes across the trip's 9 days, even though a clock change happens in the middle of it, which is the case's authored Twist (see FACILITATOR.md); (2) driving a rental car into the low-emission/congestion zones of both London and Paris carries real, separate daily/one-time fees (Congestion Charge + ULEZ; the Crit'Air sticker) that the original docx never mentioned but that a real Option-A pitch cannot honestly omit from a 'total cost of transportation' as the boilerplate literally requires ('ticket costs, gas, car rental, etc.').

modeling_assumptions.text: Fuel economy for the rental car (Appendix A, Modeling Assumption A1): 40 miles per imperial gallon, since the exact make/model of an 'economy class' booking isn't guaranteed until pickup and isn't given anywhere in this case.

The trip's calendar dates are mapped to 2027 (Appendix E, Modeling Assumption E1) so Day 3 lands on the real 2027 UK/EU clock-change date, keeping the case's own 'a few weeks away' framing forward-looking for a student reading it after August 2026 -- the real-world clock-change mechanics this case tests are the same regardless of which year a family actually books this trip.

Metro ride count (Appendix C, Modeling Assumption C1): 6 single rides per person per full city-sightseeing day, since the sisters' exact stops within London and Paris are their own itinerary choice and no route is given.

Channel-crossing baseline for a single option-vs-option comparison number (Appendix D, Modeling Assumption D1): the moderate ferry price band (~£120 each way) rather than a higher point in the Eurotunnel's range, reasoning that a trip booked only a few weeks out is unlikely to land the cheapest advance fare on either crossing.

deliverables.text: A total transportation cost table for your chosen option, converting every GBP/EUR line item (Appendices A-D) to USD at a single stated exchange rate (Appendix E), with a grand total for the full nine-day trip.

A complete, timed itinerary for your chosen option covering all nine days: departure time, arrival time, and true elapsed travel time for every intercity leg, correctly accounting for the one clock change that falls mid-trip (Appendix E). Rail choosers name the specific train service per leg; car choosers name the Channel crossing (Appendix D) and state what happens to the car during the London and Paris city days (Appendix C).
A percent breakdown of your chosen option's total cost (from D1), displayed as an original pie chart, by major category (intercity tickets/rental, Channel crossing, city transit, city driving fees).

A bar graph comparing your chosen option's total cost against your best estimate of the other option's total cost, broken out by at least three matching cost categories, using the same appendix data your sister would use.

balance.argument_a: Option A (car) totals $1,236.06 for both sisters -- $618.03 each -- $118.93 (10.65%) MORE than rail, once the case's own Appendix C rule (city metro fares apply to both options, since both sisters get around London and Paris by metro/subway regardless of how they got between cities) is actually applied to Option A's total, and once S14/S17/S26's corrected real fares are used. The $243.00 rental (£20/day x 9 days) and one round-trip Channel crossing ($324.00, 2 x £120.00) still buy full control over the Warner Bros. Studio/Stonehenge day and the Groningen day trip, both awkward by public transit alone, plus no risk of missing a Eurostar connection with heavy backpacks -- and it's still one vehicle cost split two ways, not two full sets of intercity tickets, even though it's the more expensive choice on cost alone.
balance.argument_b: Option B (rail) totals $1,117.13 for both sisters -- $558.57 each -- $118.93 (10.65%) LESS than the car, once Option A is correctly charged for city metro fares too (Appendix C: "Getting around inside London and Paris -- both options use this") on top of S14/S17's corrected fares (S14 Paris-Amsterdam €124.72, S17 Brussels-London £52.00 one-way). Rail never pays for an idle day: Option A's $324.00 round-trip Channel crossing, its $243.00 rental, and its idle-city costs -- London's £104.60 bundle ($141.21, Congestion Charge + ULEZ + parking) and Paris's €60.00 bundle ($69.60, Crit'Air sticker + parking) -- all accrue on days the car just sits in a garage, on top of the SAME $171.43 metro fares rail also pays -- so rail's cost tracks distance actually traveled, nothing else, and stays the cheaper option overall.
balance.margin_basis: Total transportation cost in USD for both sisters together, one option vs. the other, computed from every appendix line item at the stated exchange rates (Appendix E). See derived{} for the full worked total; see sensitivity_model.py for the runnable model.
balance.stability: See sensitivity_model.py FLEX sweep. The three genuine modeling assumptions (MA1 fuel economy, MA3 metro ride count, MA4 crossing-price baseline) are flexed +/-50% by Tier 2 probe 5; the cited appendix prices, distances, and exchange rates themselves are cited data, not assumptions, and are stress-tested by probe 6 (data decay) instead, per skills/case-readiness/SKILL.md's P5 doctrine. This QA pass (2026-08-18) found and fixed a real modeling bug: Option A's total was missing city metro costs entirely, even though case.md's Appendix C header states plainly that both options use the same in-city metro system. Correcting that (Option A: +$171.43) alongside the already-correct S14/S17/S26 fixes puts the honest margin back at 10.65% (Rail cheaper), reversing the prior (buggy) 4.93% Car-cheaper reading. Under the corrected model, only ONE of the three flex dials still flips the verdict at either end of its +/-50% sweep -- ferry_crossing_gbp_each_way at -50% (Car becomes cheaper) -- versus all three flipping under the buggy model; rental_mpg_imperial and metro_rides_per_person_per_day no longer flip the verdict at either end now that Option A correctly carries its own metro cost. Disclosed, not eliminated, in sensitivity_disclosure[] below. This remains a case where the honest picture (10.65%, comfortably under the SPEC.md Section 2 20% cap) is reported as found, not retuned toward a rounder number.

sensitivity_note: A family-budgeting/logistics case with no illness/death/money-hardship content. The genuine sensitivity: MA1 (rental fuel economy), MA3 (metro ride count), and MA4 (Channel crossing baseline price) are all estimates in ranges the case discloses honestly rather than single hard facts -- see FACILITATOR.md's sensitivity note and sensitivity_model.py. Before the 2026-08-18 P6 data-decay refresh, only MA4 flipped the D1 verdict under Tier 2 probe 5's +/-50% sweep at a 12.25% margin. That refresh corrected four real-world pricing errors (S1, S15, S22, S23), narrowing the margin to 3.81% (Rail cheaper), with all three assumptions then flipping the verdict. A later pass corrected three more sourcing errors (S14, S17, S26) but simultaneously introduced a real modeling bug -- Option A's total silently dropped the city metro cost that case.md's Appendix C explicitly says both options pay -- which made the case appear to flip to Car cheaper by 4.93%. This 2026-08-18 QA pass caught and fixed that bug (restoring Option A's metro cost) while independently re-confirming S14/S17/S26 remain correct on direct re-fetch: the honest current margin is 10.65%, Rail cheaper, with only ferry_crossing_gbp_each_way (MA4) still flipping the verdict at one end of its +/-50% sweep -- rental_mpg_imperial and metro_rides_per_person_per_day no longer flip it now that both options correctly carry the same metro cost. Disclosed, not eliminated, in sensitivity_disclosure[] below, because the honest reason MA4 flips is that a real, live-market future Channel-crossing price genuinely cannot be pinned down weeks ahead of booking -- narrowing the stated baseline further to dodge the flex would misrepresent that real-world volatility, not fix a modeling error.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The Channel-crossing price (MA4, Appendix D) is a single representative point picked from a genuinely wide, live-market range (Eurotunnel Le Shuttle from £69 up to roughly £284, ferry crossings £80-£193 one-way per a live GBP-denominated UK site, S26) that swings by date, time of day, and how far ahead it's booked. A trip booked only a few weeks out, as this case's own premise states, could land anywhere in that band, and the actual price for this specific future crossing cannot be known today by any amount of research -- the same forecast-shaped uncertainty as a future airfare or hotel rate (see Family Trip's fare_per_leg_usd/hotel_rate_per_night_usd disclosures), not a research gap that a better source would close. Flips the verdict at -50% flex (Car becomes cheaper) against the corrected 10.65% Rail-cheaper base.
